chunks: From him, from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

When a man accuses his wife of adultery, he does not perform li'an with her until he says: 'I saw between her legs a man committing adultery with her.' We have completed what relates to this chapter in our Great Book, and what we have mentioned is sufficient, God willing, and this adds clarification.

key_terms.بَيْنَ رِجْلَيْهَا: between her legs (indicating the specific act of intercourse)
key_terms.قَذَفَ: to accuse or throw (words) at, specifically in the context of accusing a spouse of adultery
key_terms.يُلَاعِنُهَا: he performs li'an with her (mutual imprecation)

ai.seo_question: What specific statement must a husband make for li'an to be valid in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Isfahani clarifies that for li'an to be valid, the husband's accusation must be specific, requiring him to declare he saw the act of adultery 'between her legs,' a detail emphasized by the narrator Hammad ibn al-Halabi. The reference to al-Kafi indicates this ruling is part of a broader jurisprudential discussion on whether denying paternity is a prerequisite for li'an, a key debate in Shia fiqh regarding the establishment of lineage and divorce. The specificity of the visual witness distinguishes this from general accusations, ensuring the imprecation is grounded in concrete evidence of the act itself.
